- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts rise sharply, cap the upward slope to avoid overshoot after spikes.
- If official supply net is negative and sentiment is neutral or bearish, model should not overcorrect upward — expect mean reversion toward lower range.
- After a spike in price (e.g., >75), model should reduce forecast slope for next 5–7 days to avoid lagged overreaction.
- When official events are low (few events, small net supply change), model should not overreact — forecast should be anchored to recent 7–10 day mean.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model should avoid linear extrapolation — use smoothing or weighted average of recent sentiment shifts.
- For low-event periods, forecast should be conservative — avoid upward drift unless sentiment is strongly bullish and supply is constrained.
- If true outcome shows sharp drop after spike, model should adjust downward slope in next 3–5 days to reflect mean reversion.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and supply net is negative, model should not forecast upward — expect price to stabilize or decline.
- If model forecasts are consistently above true outcome by >5% over 3–5 days, reduce forecast slope by 10–15% to avoid overconfidence bias.
- For low-event periods with high sentiment, model should not ignore recent price volatility — use 3–5 day moving average to filter noise.
